meta.title: Water Challenge, game dataset
meta.basis: Global averages unless stated otherwise. Total water footprint = green + blue + grey.
meta.units_note: impact_unit is one of 'L/kg', 'L/L', 'L per unit'. When 'L per unit', unit_detail states exactly what the unit is. Never compare an L/kg row directly with an L per unit row without converting.
meta.research_caveat: In this environment direct page fetching (WebFetch/curl) was blocked for every domain, including waterfootprint.org, hess.copernicus.org and usgs.gov. All verification was done through web search result summaries, not by opening the primary PDFs. Confidence ratings reflect that: 'high' = the exact figure was returned verbatim in search results and matches the canonical Water Footprint Network value; 'medium' = corroborated approximately or by a single source, or sources disagree; 'low' = not confirmed online, relying on recall.

primary_sources.citation: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2010/2011, 'The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products', Value of Water Research Report No. 47, UNESCO-IHE; peer-reviewed as Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci. 15: 1577-1600

Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2010/2012, 'The green, blue and grey water footprint of farm animals and animal products', Value of Water Research Report No. 48, UNESCO-IHE; peer-reviewed as Ecosystems 15: 401-415

meta.derived_from: water-data.json v1.0, compiled 2026-08-06, 69 rows, all of them carried over here

pools.per-kg: Foods and goods sold by weight. Every card reads per kg.
pools.per-unit: One of the thing: one egg, one cup, one shower, one flush, one wash cycle, one pair of jeans.
pools.per-litre: Drinks priced by volume. Reference only, not played, see excluded_reason on each row.

meta.units_rule: A round only ever pairs two items that share the same basis and the same pool. Per-kg is never compared with per-unit, and never with per-litre. Every card states its unit on screen.
meta.near_tie_rule: If two items are within 10% of each other the pairing is dropped and another is drawn, because a near-tie is not a fair question.
meta.field_note: Field names follow cards.csv (the Carbon Challenge dataset): title, sub, category, emoji, impact, comment. `impact` is litres of fresh water. Unlike carbon, water figures come on three different bases, so every card also carries `basis` and `pool` and the game only ever pairs two cards from the same pool. `in_play: false` marks reference-only rows.
meta.voice: Every title, desc, comment or intro here is read by a player and is written as Envie speaking. See CLAUDE.md and _DESIGNS/envie-voice-and-text-rewrite-guide.md: plain short sentences, no em-dashes, European spelling, no emoji, facts and sources untouched.

explainer.title: Green, blue and grey water
explainer.intro: I learned a water footprint is really three different things added together. They are not interchangeable.
explainer.green: Green water is the rain a plant drinks straight out of the soil. It is free, it is local, and it is usually the biggest part of a food's footprint.
explainer.blue: Blue water is what we pump or divert from rivers, lakes and groundwater to irrigate crops or run factories. This is the part that can actually drain a river, and it's the one that worries me most.
explainer.grey: Grey water is not water used, it is water dirtied: the amount of clean water it would take to dilute the fertiliser and other pollution from making something, back to a safe level.

cards.title: Beef
cards.comment: Only about 1% is water the cow actually drinks. Almost all of it grows the feed. That reframed beef for me.

cards.title: Lamb (sheep meat)
cards.comment: Sheep drink far less than cattle, yet lamb still comes in second thirstiest of the common meats. Wasn't the order I'd have guessed.

cards.title: Pork
cards.comment: Pigs convert feed to meat faster than cattle, and that cuts pork's water bill by about 60%. Efficiency you can taste, apparently.

cards.title: Chicken
cards.comment: Chicken is the thriftiest common meat, roughly a quarter of beef's water per kilogram. Good news if you like it grilled.

cards.title: Eggs
cards.comment: A kilo of eggs costs less water than a kilo of chicken meat, from that very same bird. Handy to know.

cards.title: One egg
cards.comment: One egg hides about 196 litres, more than a bath and a half. Didn't see that coming from something so small.
cards.source: Derived from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012 (3,265 L/kg x 0.06 kg)

cards.title: Butter
cards.comment: It takes roughly 18 litres of milk to make one kilo of butter, which explains the high figure.

cards.title: Cheese
cards.comment: Cheese concentrates milk about tenfold, so its water footprint triples milk's per kilogram, kilo for kilo.
cards.note: Sources disagree: WFN gives 3,178 L/kg; some compilations quote 5,000-5,990 L/kg depending on cheese type and milk-to-cheese ratio.

cards.title: Milk
cards.excluded_reason: Sold by volume, so it sits on a per-litre basis and cannot share a round with per-kg or per-unit items. Only four items share that basis, too few for a fair pool, so the per-litre rows are reference only. The 250 ml glass of milk carries the same figure into play.
cards.comment: Every litre of milk in the fridge represents about a thousand litres out in the fields. Small carton, big story.

cards.title: Glass of milk
cards.comment: A single glass of milk carries more hidden water than three full baths. I looked twice at that one.
cards.source: Derived from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012 (1,020 L/L x 0.25 L)

cards.title: Chocolate
cards.comment: Kilo for kilo, chocolate is thirstier than beef. Cocoa trees are the reason, and I wasn't ready for that.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network Product Gallery (from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011)

cards.title: Cocoa beans
cards.comment: Cocoa has the largest water footprint of any major crop measured by the Water Footprint Network. Top of a list I wasn't expecting.

cards.title: Coffee (roasted beans)
cards.comment: Roasting drives the number up: green beans sit at 15,897 L/kg, roasted ones climb to nearly 19,000. All that from one bean.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (18,925 L/kg roasted; 15,897 L/kg green)

cards.title: Coffee (one cup)
cards.comment: One small cup of coffee took about 132 litres to reach you, roughly 1,000 times its own volume. My cup felt heavier after that.
cards.unit_detail: per 125 ml cup (about 7 g of roasted coffee)

cards.title: Tea (dried leaves)
cards.comment: Tea leaves need less than half the water of coffee beans, and you use fewer grams per cup too. Tea's quietly winning this one.

cards.title: Tea (one cup)
cards.comment: Swapping a coffee for a tea saves about 105 litres, roughly a bath and a bit. Small swap, decent saving.
cards.unit_detail: per 250 ml cup (about 3 g of dried tea)

cards.title: Rice (milled, white)
cards.comment: Rice is the single biggest user of irrigation water on Earth, ahead of wheat and cotton. A grain topping that list took me by surprise.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (paddy rice 1,673 L/kg)

cards.title: Wheat
cards.comment: About 70% of wheat's water is rain the plant drinks straight from the soil, not irrigation. Mostly the sky's doing, not a pump's.

cards.title: Bread
cards.comment: A standard 800 g loaf carries around 1,290 litres, mostly rain that fell on a wheat field long before it was bread.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (derived wheat products)

cards.title: Maize (corn)
cards.comment: Maize is the most efficient major cereal per kilogram, beating both wheat and rice. Fair play to the humble cob.

cards.title: Potatoes
cards.comment: Potatoes are about 80% water themselves, and one of the thriftiest staples you can grow. Good spud, honestly.

cards.title: Pasta (dry)
cards.comment: Dry pasta costs slightly more water than the wheat it came from. Drying it off loses mass, which nudges the number up.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (derived crop products)

cards.title: Soybeans
cards.comment: Most soy never reaches a plate at all. It is grown to feed livestock, not people. That one stuck with me.

cards.title: Tofu
cards.comment: Tofu needs roughly a sixth of beef's water for the same weight of protein-rich food. Worth remembering next time I'm shopping.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network Product Gallery (from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011)

cards.title: Lentils
cards.comment: Lentils look thirsty per kilogram, but they are sold dry. Cooked, they roughly triple in weight, so the real number per plate is far lower.

cards.title: Almonds (shelled)
cards.comment: Shelling doubles the figure: half an almond's harvested weight is shell you throw straight away. That's a lot of waste for a snack.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (in-shell about 8,050 L/kg)

cards.title: Walnuts (shelled)
cards.comment: Walnuts come in at roughly half of almonds. Nuts vary a lot more than I expected.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (in-shell about 4,920 L/kg)

cards.title: Peanuts (groundnuts, in shell)
cards.comment: Peanuts are legumes, not nuts, and they drink about a sixth of what almonds do. Good value, all round.

cards.title: Apples
cards.comment: Apple trees are perennial, so their water use is spread over decades of harvests. Patient plants, patient number.

cards.title: One apple
cards.comment: One apple comes to about 125 litres, roughly one and a half baths for a piece of fruit you can eat in five minutes.
cards.source: Derived from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011 (822 L/kg x 0.15 kg)

cards.title: Bananas
cards.comment: Bananas grow in the wet tropics, so almost all their water is rain rather than irrigation. The sky does the heavy lifting there.

cards.title: Oranges
cards.comment: Eating the orange beats drinking it: juice needs several fruits squeezed into one glass. Whole fruit wins again.

cards.title: Orange juice
cards.excluded_reason: Sold by volume, so it sits on a per-litre basis and cannot share a round with per-kg or per-unit items. Only four items share that basis, too few for a fair pool, so the per-litre rows are reference only.
cards.comment: A 200 ml glass of orange juice hides about 200 litres. Juicing really concentrates the footprint.
cards.source: Hoekstra 2008, 'The water footprint of food', WFN

cards.title: Tomatoes
cards.comment: Tomatoes are one of the lightest footprint foods there is, about a bath and a half per kilo. Nice one, tomatoes.

cards.title: Lettuce
cards.comment: A whole kilo of lettuce costs less water than a single egg. That one still surprises me.
cards.note: Older Chapagain & Hoekstra (2004) compilations list lettuce at about 130 L/kg.

cards.title: Cabbage
cards.comment: Cabbage stores well for months, so almost none of its water goes to waste through spoilage. Practical vegetable, that.
cards.note: Older WFN compilations list cabbage at about 200 L/kg.

cards.title: Cucumber
cards.comment: A cucumber is about 96% water itself, yet takes only around 350 litres per kilo to grow. Mostly water growing more water.

cards.title: Avocado
cards.comment: One 200 g avocado runs to about 400 litres, nearly ten times a tomato of the same weight. That changed how I see brunch.

cards.title: Olives
cards.comment: Olive trees survive on very little rain, but it takes about five kilos of olives to press one litre of oil. The tree is thrifty, the oil is not.

cards.title: Olive oil
cards.comment: Olive oil is the thirstiest common cooking oil, roughly triple palm oil per kilogram. My favourite topped a chart I wasn't hoping for.

cards.title: Palm oil
cards.comment: Oil palms yield more oil per hectare than any other crop, which keeps their water figure surprisingly low.

cards.title: Sugar cane
cards.comment: Raw cane looks cheap in water terms, but only about a tenth of it ends up as sugar. The rest is stalk and juice lost along the way.

cards.title: Sugar beet
cards.comment: Beet grows in cool, rainy places, so it needs about a third less water than cane. Location does a lot of the work.

cards.title: Refined sugar (from cane)
cards.comment: A single teaspoon of sugar carries roughly seven litres of hidden water. Never looked at my tea the same way since.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (derived crop products)

cards.title: Beer
cards.excluded_reason: Sold by volume, so it sits on a per-litre basis and cannot share a round with per-kg or per-unit items. Only four items share that basis, too few for a fair pool, so the per-litre rows are reference only. The 250 ml glass of beer carries the same figure into play.
cards.comment: Over 90% of beer's footprint is the barley field, not the brewery. The pint is the easy part.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network (from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, barley products)

cards.title: Beer (one glass)
cards.comment: One glass of beer equals about 300 glasses of water once you count the barley behind it. Puts a pint in perspective.
cards.source: Derived from WFN beer figure (298 L/L x 0.25 L)

cards.title: Wine
cards.excluded_reason: Sold by volume, so it sits on a per-litre basis and cannot share a round with per-kg or per-unit items. Only four items share that basis, too few for a fair pool, so the per-litre rows are reference only. The 125 ml glass of wine carries the same figure into play.
cards.comment: Wine costs roughly three times beer per litre, because grapes give less juice per plant. Grapes work harder for less.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (wine grapes 869 m3/tonne)

cards.title: Wine (one glass)
cards.comment: A small glass of wine hides more water than a full bath. That one made me pause mid sip.
cards.note: Older Chapagain & Hoekstra (2004) figures put a 125 ml glass at about 120 litres.
cards.source: Derived from WFN wine figure (869 L/L x 0.125 L)

cards.title: Cotton (lint)
cards.comment: Cotton is the thirstiest non-food crop, and it grows mostly in countries that are already dry. That combination worries me a bit.
cards.note: Seed cotton (unginned) is roughly 3,600 L/kg; the 10,000 figure is for processed lint/fabric.
cards.source: Chapagain, Hoekstra et al. 2006, WFN Report 18 (cotton consumption)

cards.title: Cotton t-shirt
cards.comment: One t-shirt is about 2,500 litres, roughly what one person drinks in three years. I'll think of that next time I'm shopping.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network / Chapagain et al. 2006

cards.title: Pair of jeans
cards.comment: Jeans cost about 8,000 litres, and most of it fell as rain on a cotton field long before the denim did.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network / Chapagain et al. 2006
cards.unit_detail: per one 800 g pair of cotton jeans

cards.title: Pair of leather shoes
cards.comment: Leather shoes inherit the cow's whole footprint. The tanning itself is only a tiny share of the number.
cards.note: Estimates vary widely: 8,000 L/pair is the commonly cited WFN figure, some sources quote 14,000-16,600 L/pair depending on leather weight allocated.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network (bovine leather about 17,100 L/kg)
cards.unit_detail: per one pair of bovine-leather shoes

cards.title: Sheet of A4 paper
cards.comment: Most of a sheet's water is not the mill at all. It is rain the tree drank years before it became paper.
cards.source: Van Oel & Hoekstra 2010, WFN Report 46 (300-2,600 m3/tonne, about 2-13 L per A4 sheet)
cards.unit_detail: per one A4 sheet of 80 gsm printing paper

cards.title: Smartphone
cards.comment: Chip fabs rinse silicon wafers in ultra-pure water hundreds of times per device. Never thought of a phone as thirsty before.
cards.source: Friends of the Earth 'Mind Your Step' report; commonly quoted 12,000-13,000 L
cards.unit_detail: per one smartphone, whole manufacturing chain

cards.title: Car
cards.comment: Over 95% of a car's water is spent before you ever turn the key. All of it gone before the first drive.
cards.note: Older popular figures of 400,000 L per car come from different, broader virtual-water accounting and are not supported by the peer-reviewed LCA.
cards.source: Berger et al. 2012, Environ. Sci. Technol., 'Water Footprint of European Cars'
cards.unit_detail: per one mid-size car, production phase (range 52,000-83,000 L)

cards.title: Shower (per minute)
cards.excluded_reason: A flow rate rather than a single act, and the 8-minute shower row already represents showering in the per-unit pool. Kept here because the reality checks and the actions list both use the 9 litres a minute figure.
cards.comment: A power shower can hit 15 litres a minute, nearly double a standard head. Worth knowing before you crank it up.

cards.title: Shower (typical, 8 minutes)
cards.comment: Showers are the single biggest water use in a typical home, about a quarter of the total. Mine included, probably.
cards.source: Derived from Waterwise UK flow rate; Energy Saving Trust 'At Home with Water'

cards.title: Bath
cards.comment: A bath and a long shower are surprisingly close. Whichever one runs longer loses, simple as that.

cards.title: Toilet flush (old single-flush)
cards.comment: Old cisterns sent up to 13 litres of drinking quality water down the drain with every flush. Straight down for nothing.
cards.source: European Commission water efficiency study; USGS Water Science School

cards.title: Toilet flush (modern dual-flush, full)
cards.comment: Dual flush cisterns cut each flush by more than half, and most people never even notice.
cards.source: European Commission water efficiency standards study

cards.title: Toilet flush (modern dual-flush, half)
cards.comment: The small button uses 3 litres, about one glass of milk's worth of real water. A tiny button doing real work.
cards.source: European Commission water efficiency standards study

cards.title: Dishwasher cycle
cards.comment: A full dishwasher beats hand washing. The tap alone runs at about 6 litres a minute if you leave it going.
cards.unit_detail: per cycle, modern full-size machine on eco

cards.title: Washing machine cycle
cards.comment: Machines have quietly cut their water use by a third since the late 1990s. Nobody throws a party for that, but they should.
cards.source: APPLiA Europe statistical report 2022-2023 (about 46 L/cycle in 2022, down from 65 L in the late 1990s)

cards.title: Brushing teeth with the tap running
cards.sub: brushing your teeth with the tap running
cards.comment: Two minutes of running tap is 12 litres, twice what a modern toilet flush uses. I'm guilty of that one.
cards.source: Waterwise UK / Cambridge Water (tap runs at about 6 L/min)

cards.title: Brushing teeth with the tap off
cards.sub: brushing your teeth with the tap off
cards.comment: Turning the tap off while brushing cuts that step by more than 90%. Small habit, big drop.
cards.unit_detail: per brushing, wetting brush plus a glass to rinse

cards.title: Dripping tap (per day)
cards.sub: one dripping tap for a day
cards.comment: A single slow drip wastes over 5,000 litres a year, about 70 baths down the drain for nothing.
cards.source: USGS drip calculator; UK water utility guidance
cards.unit_detail: per day, one slowly dripping tap (range 3-30 L/day)

cards.title: Household water use per person per day (Europe)
cards.sub: one day of home water use in Europe
cards.comment: Europeans use about 124 litres a day at home, less than one cup of coffee's hidden water. Puts my own day in perspective.
cards.source: European Environment Agency / Eurostat-based estimates (range about 120-145 L)
cards.unit_detail: per person per day, direct domestic use

cards.title: Household water use per person per day (USA)
cards.sub: one day of home water use in the USA
cards.comment: Americans use roughly two and a half times as much water at home as Europeans. That gap is bigger than I expected.
cards.source: US EPA WaterSense / USGS Water Science School
cards.unit_detail: per person per day, direct domestic use (82 US gallons)

cards.title: Minimum for basic human needs
cards.sub: one person's basic daily water needs
cards.comment: Fifty litres a day covers drinking, cooking and washing, about one seventh of the average US home use. That's survival, not comfort.
cards.source: WHO, 'How much water is needed in emergencies' (50-100 L/person/day)
cards.unit_detail: per person per day, WHO guidance for drinking, cooking and hygiene

actions.action: Swap one beef meal a week for chicken, or for beans and lentils.
actions.number: A 200 g beef portion is 3,083 L; the same portion of chicken is 865 L.
actions.arithmetic: (15,415 - 4,325) L/kg x 0.2 kg = 2,218 L saved per meal; x 52 weeks = about 115,000 L a year
actions.framing: Biggest single lever in the whole dataset. One meal, not your whole diet.

actions.saving: 3,178 L per wasted kilo of cheese
actions.action: Eat what you buy: finish the cheese, the bread and the leftovers before they go off.
actions.number: A wasted 1 kg block of cheese throws away 3,178 L; a wasted 800 g loaf, 1,286 L.
actions.framing: Food you already own is the cheapest water saving available.

actions.action: Get one more year out of the clothes you own before replacing them.
actions.number: One t-shirt is 2,495 L and one pair of jeans is 8,000 L.
actions.arithmetic: 2,495 + 8,000 = 10,495 L for a single shirt-and-jeans replacement avoided
actions.framing: One garment not bought beats months of shorter showers.

actions.action: Turn the tap off while you brush.
actions.number: 12 L becomes 1 L, twice a day.
actions.framing: Costs nothing, and it is about three t-shirts' worth of water a year.

actions.action: Take two minutes off your shower.
actions.number: A standard showerhead runs at 9 L a minute.
actions.arithmetic: 9 L/min x 2 min x 365 = 6,570 L a year
actions.framing: Same order of magnitude as the toothbrush habit. Small, but it compounds daily.

actions.number: A slow drip is about 15 L a day.
actions.arithmetic: 15 L/day x 365 = 5,475 L a year, roughly 68 baths
actions.framing: A ten-minute job that runs in the background for the rest of the year.

comparisons.line: One beef burger (150 g patty) = about 32 showers.
One cup of coffee = 11 tooth-brushings with the tap left running.
comparisons.arithmetic: 132 L per cup / 12 L per 2-min running-tap brushing = 11.0
relates_to: Brushing teeth with the tap running

comparisons.line: One cotton t-shirt = 35 showers, or 20 days of a European's entire home water use.
comparisons.arithmetic: 2,495 L / 72 L = 34.7 showers; 2,495 / 124 L per person per day = 20.1 days
relates_to: Household water use per person per day (Europe)

comparisons.line: One pair of jeans = 65 days of everything one European does with water at home.
comparisons.arithmetic: 8,000 L / 124 L per person per day = 64.5 days
relates_to: Household water use per person per day (Europe)

comparisons.line: One egg = 33 flushes of a modern dual-flush toilet.
One kilo of cheese = 64 washing-machine cycles.
One kilo of beef = 50 days of an average American's home water use.
comparisons.arithmetic: 15,415 L / 310 L per person per day = 49.7 days
relates_to: Household water use per person per day (USA)

comparisons.line: A small glass of wine = more water than a full bath.
comparisons.arithmetic: 109 L per 125 ml glass vs 80 L per bath = 1.36x

comparisons.line: A whole kilo of lettuce = 3 baths. A kilo of lamb = 130 baths.
Swapping one coffee for one tea saves as much water as skipping a bath and a third.
comparisons.arithmetic: 132 L - 27 L = 105 L saved; 105 / 80 L per bath = 1.31
